questions.q: What are the three recognized authentication factor categories?
options: Something you know, something you have, something you are
Something you remember, something you own, something you say
Username, password, and email address
Local login, network login, and remote login
questions.explain: Every authentication method falls into knowledge, possession, or inherence — something you know, have, or are.

questions.q: Why doesn't a password plus a security-question answer count as true multi-factor authentication?
options: Both are the same factor — something you know — so they don't add real independent protection
Security questions are not allowed by any authentication standard
It actually does count as true MFA
Passwords can only be paired with biometrics, never with questions
questions.explain: Real MFA requires factors from different categories; two knowledge-based secrets don't give you that independence.

questions.q: What is a TOTP code, as generated by an authenticator app?
options: A time-based one-time code that regenerates every 30 seconds from a shared secret
A permanent password that never changes
A code sent exclusively over SMS
A biometric scan converted into a code
questions.explain: TOTP stands for Time-based One-Time Password, computed on-device from a secret established at enrollment.

questions.q: Why is SMS-based MFA considered weaker than an authenticator app or hardware key?
options: It's vulnerable to SIM swapping and interception on the aging SS7 signaling network
SMS messages are always sent unencrypted in plain view to the public internet
Phones cannot receive SMS messages reliably
It is actually the strongest method of the three
questions.explain: SIM swapping lets an attacker port a victim's number to their own SIM, and SS7 weaknesses can allow interception — both bypass SMS codes.

questions.q: Why are hardware security keys like a YubiKey considered phishing-resistant?
options: Their cryptographic challenge is tied to the real site's domain, so a fake lookalike site can't use them
They store the user's password in plain text for faster lookup
They only work over SMS, which cannot be phished
They require no authentication at all once plugged in
questions.explain: The key's challenge-response check is bound to the legitimate domain, so a convincing fake login page still can't complete it.
